nodes.label: The early caliphate (Rashidun & Umayyad)
nodes.full: The new Arab-Islamic state centred first on Medina, then on Kufa and Damascus, which absorbed the Sasanian Empire and governed the Gulf coast as an appendage of Basra.
nodes.src: background — al-Baladhuri, 'Futuh al-Buldan'.

nodes.label: The Church of the East under Islam
nodes.full: The Catholicos and the wider church, now living under Muslim rule near Ctesiphon, to which the Gulf bishops still owed — and for thirty years refused — obedience.
nodes.src: background — the Synodicon Orientale; Brock on the church under early Islam.

nodes.label: Basra
nodes.full: The garrison city founded in 638 that became the administrative and naval capital of the Gulf, the base of Ibadi scholarship, and the city the Omani Azd resettled into in numbers.
nodes.src: background — the foundation and early role of Basra (al-Baladhuri).

nodes.label: The Abbasid revolution
nodes.full: The overthrow of the Umayyads out of Khurasan, whose confusion let the Omani Ibadis proclaim their first imam — and whose victors then sent an army to destroy him.
nodes.src: background — Sharon, 'Black Banners from the East' (1983).

nodes.label: Eastern Arabia governed from Basra
nodes.full: Under the Umayyads and early Abbasids, Bahrain and Oman were administered as appendages of Basra, their governors appointed by the Iraqi viceroy. Distance from the centre made both regions chronically hard to hold.
nodes.src: al-Tabari and al-Baladhuri on the Basran governorship of al-Bahrayn and Oman; the Azd of Oman as a major faction in Basra itself.

nodes.label: Al-Julanda ibn Masud, first imam of Oman
nodes.full: As the Umayyad state collapsed, the Omani Ibadis elected al-Julanda ibn Masud as imam — the first attempt to realise their ideal of a community governed by an elected, deposable religious leader. An Abbasid army killed him within two years.
nodes.src: Ibadi chronicle tradition (al-Salimi, 'Tuhfat al-Ayan'); Wilkinson, 'The Imamate Tradition of Oman' (1987). Killed at the battle of Julfar, 751.

nodes.label: The Ridda war in Bahrain — the siege of Juwatha
nodes.full: On the Prophet's death much of Bahrain renounced Islam under al-Hutam and a claimant king. The Muslim loyalists, chiefly the Abd al-Qays, were besieged at Juwatha until a relief force under al-Ala al-Hadrami broke the revolt.
nodes.src: al-Tabari on the Ridda in al-Bahrayn; the siege of Juwatha and the battle that followed, 633; al-Ala ibn al-Hadrami's command.

nodes.label: The Battle of Dibba
nodes.full: The Omani apostasy under Laqit ibn Malik, 'Dhu al-Taj', ended at Dibba, where a caliphal army with Julanda allies destroyed the rebel host. A vast early cemetery at Dibba is traditionally linked to the dead of the battle.
nodes.src: al-Baladhuri and al-Tabari on the Omani Ridda and Dibba, 633; the Dibba cemetery excavated by the Sharjah and Fujairah authorities.

nodes.label: The Abbasid conquest of Ibadi Oman
nodes.full: An Abbasid expeditionary force under Khazim ibn Khuzayma crushed the first Ibadi imamate at Julfar, killing Imam al-Julanda ibn Masud. Ibadi self-government in Oman would have to be rebuilt from scratch a generation later.
nodes.src: al-Tabari on Khazim ibn Khuzayma's campaign; Ibadi accounts of the martyrdom of al-Julanda ibn Masud (al-Salimi).

nodes.label: Governing the Gulf from Basra
nodes.full: Under the Rashidun and Umayyads the Gulf coast was run as an appendage of Basra: a governor (ʿāmil) collected the ṣadaqa and the jizya, confirmed tribal leaders and left the interior largely alone. Distance made the arrangement loose, and both Bahrain and Oman slipped in and out of real caliphal control.
nodes.src: al-Baladhuri and al-Tabari on the Basran administration of al-Bahrayn and Oman; the ṣadaqa/jizya assessment of the region.

nodes.label: The Beth Qatraye schism
nodes.full: For nearly thirty years the bishops of the Gulf refused obedience to the Catholicos in Ctesiphon, running their church as an autonomous body. The dispute — over authority, not doctrine — shows how far the Gulf Christian community had grown into its own identity.
nodes.src: The schism and its resolution at the 676 synod (Synodicon Orientale); Brock, 'Syriac writers from Beth Qatraye', ARAM 11–12 (1999–2000).

nodes.label: The Synod of Dayrin, 676 — canons for the Gulf churches
nodes.full: The Catholicos George I sailed to Tarut island and held a synod for the bishops of Beth Qatraye, issuing nineteen canons on clergy, marriage, inheritance and the conduct of women — and healing a decades-long schism in which the Gulf bishops had rejected his authority.
nodes.src: Acts of the Synod of Mar George (676), in Chabot, 'Synodicon Orientale' (1902); Kozah et al. (eds.), 'The Syriac Writers of Qatar' (2014).

nodes.label: Isaac of Nineveh and the Qatari ascetic tradition
nodes.full: Isaac the Syrian, the most widely read spiritual writer the Church of the East produced, was born in Beth Qatraye. His treatises on prayer, solitude and divine mercy were later translated into Greek, Arabic, Ethiopic and Slavonic and are read across Christianity to this day.
nodes.src: Isaac of Nineveh, 'Ascetical Homilies'; Brock and Kozah et al., 'The Syriac Writers of Qatar' (2014). Isaac consecrated bishop of Nineveh c.676, then withdrew to solitude.

nodes.label: The mosque of Juwatha
nodes.full: Tradition holds that the Abd al-Qays built a mosque at Juwatha soon after accepting Islam and defending it through the Ridda, and that it was the first place outside Medina where the Friday congregational prayer was held. Its ruined mud-brick remains are among the oldest mosque sites in the Gulf.
nodes.src: Juwatha mosque tradition in the hadith collections and al-Bakri; the standing mud-brick remains restored by the Saudi antiquities authority.

nodes.label: The Ibadi da'wa reaches Oman
nodes.full: The quietist Kharijite school that became Ibadism formed among scholars in Basra, many of them Omani Azd, and its missionaries carried it back to the Omani interior. By the early 8th century Ibadism was the framework through which Oman's tribes imagined a rightly-guided community — and the basis for the imamate they would proclaim.
nodes.src: The Basran origins of Ibadism around Jabir ibn Zayd and Abu Ubayda (Wilkinson, 'Ibadism: Origins and Early Development in Oman', 2010); the da'wa to Oman.

nodes.label: The twilight of Gulf Christianity
nodes.full: The Gulf monasteries were abandoned, one by one and without violence, through the 8th and into the 9th century. No bishop of Beth Qatraye is recorded after the early 8th century. Under dhimmi status, without new converts, the Christian population dwindled and assimilated into the Muslim majority.
nodes.src: Monastery abandonment dates from the archaeology (Carter, 'Christianity in the Gulf during the first centuries of Islam', AAE 19, 2008); the disappearance of the Beth Qatraye see from the synod records.

nodes.label: The earliest Gulf mosques
nodes.full: The first Gulf mosques were simple mud-brick prayer halls, their qibla walls later fitted with concave mihrabs. The transition can be read on the ground where a monastery is abandoned and a mosque rises in the same oasis within a generation.
nodes.src: Juwatha mosque; early Omani mosque archaeology (e.g. the mosque sequence at Bilad Sur and inland Oman); Carter (2008).

nodes.label: The last phase at Al-Qusur
nodes.full: The large church complex at Al-Qusur on Failaka was built and decorated with moulded plaster crosses in the seventh century — under Muslim rule, not before it. The finest surviving phase of Gulf Christian architecture dates from after the conquest, a reminder that the community's decline was slow.
nodes.src: Al-Qusur excavations (French/Kuwaiti mission; Bernard & Salles); the 7th-century date of the main building phase (Carter 2008).

nodes.label: From monastery to mosque
nodes.full: At several eastern Arabian oases the archaeological sequence shows a church or monastery going out of use and a mud-brick mosque built nearby within a generation or two — the physical trace of a population changing its religion, read in stratigraphy.
nodes.src: The monastery-to-mosque transition in the Gulf oasis archaeology (Carter 2008); early Omani mosque sequences.

nodes.label: Dadisho Qatraya on the solitary life
nodes.full: Dadisho of Qatar wrote commentaries on the ascetic classics — 'The Book of Abba Isaiah', the 'Paradise of the Fathers' — and a treatise on solitude that codified the theory of the hermit's life for the whole Church of the East.
nodes.src: Dadisho Qatraya, 'Commentary on Abba Isaiah' and 'On Stillness'; Kozah et al., 'An Anthology of Syriac Writers from Qatar in the Seventh Century' (2015).

nodes.label: A cluster of scholars from one small region
nodes.full: In the decades after the conquest, and largely under Muslim rule, Beth Qatraye produced Isaac of Nineveh, Dadisho, Ahob the exegete and Abraham bar Lipeh — an intellectual output out of all proportion to the region's size, and the last great flowering of Gulf Christian learning.
nodes.src: Brock, 'Syriac writers from Beth Qatraye', ARAM 11–12 (1999–2000); the 2014–15 Qatar-based edition project.

nodes.label: Abraham bar Lipeh and the last generation
nodes.full: Abraham bar Lipeh of Qatar wrote a compact commentary on the liturgy, drawing on Gabriel of Qatar's fuller work of a century before. He is among the last named writers of Beth Qatraye — the tradition closing just as the community that sustained it began to disappear.
nodes.src: Abraham bar Lipeh, 'Commentary on the Liturgical Offices' (dependent on Gabriel of Qatar); Brock, 'Syriac writers from Beth Qatraye', ARAM 11–12 (1999–2000).

nodes.label: The Indian Ocean trade under the caliphate
nodes.full: The sea route to India and China did not stop at the conquest — it was redirected to its head. Basra, and then the Persian port of Siraf, became the great emporia through which Gulf shipping reached Guangzhou, and the Omani and Sirafi merchant communities that would dominate that trade began to form.
nodes.src: The early Islamic Gulf–China trade (Chaffee, 'The Muslim Merchants of Premodern China', 2018); the rise of Basra and Siraf as the eastern trade's northern termini.

nodes.label: The Sasanian–Islamic ceramic continuum
nodes.full: The turquoise-glazed and torpedo storage jars of the late Sasanian Gulf kept being made, shipped and used, unchanged, for a century after the conquest — the archaeologists' 'Sasanian-Islamic' ware. The economy of the Gulf carried on across the political rupture with barely a visible seam.
nodes.src: D. Kennet, 'Sasanian and Islamic Pottery from Ras al-Khaimah' (2004); the 'Sasanian-Islamic' ceramic horizon as evidence of economic continuity.

nodes.label: Pearls and dates as caliphal revenue
nodes.full: The pearl banks and the al-Hasa date gardens went on producing, and the caliphal governor took his share. The wealth that had made eastern Arabia worth garrisoning for the Sasanians made it worth taxing for Basra — one reason the region was never simply let go.
nodes.src: The revenue of al-Bahrayn in the early Arabic administrative and geographical literature (al-Baladhuri; later Qudama ibn Ja'far).

nodes.label: The sewn boat under new management
nodes.full: The stitched-plank, bitumen-caulked hull that carried Sasanian trade to China went on being built in exactly the same way for the caliphate's merchants. Arab and Persian shipwrights, many of them the same families, kept the technology unbroken across the change of rulers.
nodes.src: Continuity of the sewn-boat tradition across the Sasanian–Islamic transition (Agius, 'Classic Ships of Islam', 2008).

nodes.label: The mud-brick hypostyle mosque
nodes.full: The first Gulf mosques were built with the region's oldest technique — sun-dried mud brick on a stone footing — in a new plan: a broad prayer hall of palm-trunk columns facing a qibla wall, later fitted with a concave miḥrāb. The form was simple, cheap and fast, and it spread with the faith.
nodes.src: Juwatha mosque and early Omani mosque archaeology; the hypostyle mud-brick plan of the earliest Arabian mosques (Carter 2008).

nodes.label: Syriac and Arabic in the Gulf schools
nodes.full: The Qatari writers worked in Syriac but lived among Arabic-speakers; within a century their world would be Arabic-speaking and Muslim. Their works became a bridge — several were translated into Arabic and fed into the wider Islamic-era spiritual literature.
nodes.src: The Arabic reception of Isaac of Nineveh and Dadisho; Brock on Syriac–Arabic bilingualism in Beth Qatraye.

nodes.label: The Azd of Oman migrate to Basra
nodes.full: Large numbers of the Omani Azd resettled in the new garrison city of Basra, becoming one of its dominant tribal blocs and a power in early Islamic politics. Oman's affairs and Basra's were thereafter entangled for centuries.
nodes.src: The Azd of Basra in al-Tabari and the futuh literature; Wilkinson (1987) on the Oman–Basra connection.

nodes.label: The last road to Ctesiphon
nodes.full: Even after the conquest the bishops of Beth Qatraye still owed obedience to the Catholicos of the Church of the East, now living under Muslim rule near Ctesiphon — and still, for thirty years, refused it. The 676 synod's journey to Tarut was the church's structure reasserting itself one last time before the Gulf sees faded from the record.
nodes.src: The Beth Qatraye schism and its resolution (Synodicon Orientale, Synod of 676); the Catholicos's position under early Islamic rule (Brock).

nodes.label: The rise of Islam and the Arab conquest of Persia
nodes.full: Within twenty years the new Muslim state absorbed the whole Sasanian Empire. For the Gulf coast it meant the Persian governing apparatus vanished and the region became part of a polity centred, for the first time in a millennium, on Arabia and then Iraq.
nodes.src: The battles of al-Qadisiyya (636) and Nihawand (642); the death of Yazdegerd III (651). Standard accounts in al-Tabari and al-Baladhuri.

nodes.label: The founding of Basra reorients the Gulf
nodes.full: The new garrison city of Basra became the administrative and naval capital of the Gulf, from which Bahrain and Oman were governed and toward which their tribes and trade were drawn. The Gulf's centre of gravity moved to its head.
nodes.src: Foundation of Basra under Umar, 638; its role as the base for Gulf administration and Indian Ocean expeditions (al-Baladhuri).

nodes.label: The Abbasid revolution
nodes.full: The overthrow of the Umayyads convulsed the whole caliphate. In the confusion the Omani Ibadis proclaimed their first imam — and the victorious Abbasids, once secure, sent an army to destroy him.
nodes.src: The Abbasid revolution (Sharon, 'Black Banners from the East', 1983); the Omani imamate proclaimed 749, crushed 751.

nodes.label: The solitary as a recognised way of life
nodes.full: Dadisho Qatraya's treatise 'On Stillness' gives the hermit — withdrawn, silent, outside ordinary social and family roles — a fully theorised place in the church. The Gulf helped define solitude itself as a legitimate human vocation.
nodes.src: Dadisho Qatraya, 'On Stillness / Shelya'; the anchoretic ideal in the Church of the East (Brock).

nodes.label: The 676 canons on women in church
nodes.full: Several of the Synod of Dayrin's canons concern women — barring them from certain parts of the church, regulating consecrated virgins and widows, restricting mixed gatherings. The rules are restrictive, but they document an active female presence the hierarchy felt the need to control.
nodes.src: Canons of the Synod of Mar George (676), Synodicon Orientale; discussion in the Qatar Syriac writers project (Kozah et al. 2014).

nodes.label: The dead of Dibba
nodes.full: The very large early cemetery at Dibba — thousands of simple graves — is traditionally the burial of those killed in the Ridda battle. Whatever its exact makeup, it is a rare physical trace of the human cost of the wars that fixed the Gulf inside Islam.
nodes.src: The Dibba cemetery (Sharjah and Fujairah archaeology authorities); the traditional association with the 633 battle.

nodes.label: Becoming dhimmi
nodes.full: For the Gulf's Christians, Jews and Zoroastrians, the settlements of the 620s created a new legal identity: protected non-Muslims, free to practise but taxed and subordinate. Christianity persisted in the Gulf for generations under this status before fading in the 8th–9th centuries.
nodes.src: The dhimma arrangements (Ibn Sa'd; al-Baladhuri); the slow decline of Gulf Christianity traced by Carter (2008) via the monastery abandonment dates.
